title: The Cambrian Explosion, When the First Eyes Arrived
metaDescription: Tonight goes back further than this collection ever has, past the dinosaurs and the coal forests, to a stretch of ocean more than half a billion years old.
description: Tonight goes back further than this collection ever has, past the dinosaurs, past the coal forests, to a stretch of ocean more than half a billion years old, when almost nothing alive could tell one shape from another at any distance. In a little over fifty million years, that changes completely: shells appear almost everywhere within a short window of time, an eye arrives good enough to actually see with, and an ocean that had spent three billion years mostly sitting still becomes a world of animals noticing one another for the first time.

This one touches something the channel hasn't had to touch this directly before (real predators, real defences). It's told entirely through the noticing and the answering: a shell thickening, a body curling shut, a burrow going a little deeper. Nothing here describes the moment anything actually gets caught.

Some of tonight rests on work only a year or two old, including a genuine correction to one of the most famous animals in this whole story. Its classic "armoured hunter" reputation doesn't survive contact with current evidence. Other parts are honestly, actively disputed right now: what actually set this whole event in motion is one of the oldest open questions in evolutionary biology, and nobody studying it today claims to have closed it.
You do not need to follow any of it closely. If you're asleep before the shells finish arriving, that's the intended use.

chapters.title: A Debt To Colder, Older Times

accuracy: Every factual claim traces to a named, published source, listed below. This episode leans on more recent and more actively disputed research than most, and where researchers disagree, it says so rather than picking the tidier answer.

sources.title: Why the Explosion Happened When It Did

sources.cite: Stockey, Cole, Farrell et al. (2024), Nature Geoscience — a modest, threshold-crossing rise in shallow-water oxygen, refining rather than overturning the oxygen hypothesis
Sperling & Stockey (2018), Integrative and Comparative Biology — rejects single-cause explanations; oxygen, food supply, temperature and genetics arriving together
Wood, Liu, Bowyer et al. (2019), Nature Ecology & Evolution — questions the "explosion" framing itself, arguing for a series of successive radiations
Parker (1998), Proc. Royal Society B, and Parker (2003), In the Blink of an Eye — the original "Light Switch Theory," that vision triggered the wider explosion
Schoenemann, Pärnaste & Clarkson (2017), PNAS — the oldest well-documented image-forming eye, ~530 million years old
Current standing: a contested, largely marginalised framing now, folded into the broader predation story rather than credited as the one mechanism
Bicknell & Paterson (2018), Biological Reviews — the most direct Cambrian-focused study of predation's role, and a genuinely cautious one
Bicknell et al. (2024/2025), Current Biology — direct fossil evidence: over 200 shells showing thickness increasing in step with predator-drilling frequency
Note: "escalation" as a named concept belongs to Vermeij's much later work on the Mesozoic Marine Revolution, not the Cambrian — the episode is careful not to misattribute it
Daley & Edgecombe (2014), Journal of Paleontology — Anomalocaris's real size (mostly ~25cm, not the old "2 metres" figure)
Bicknell, Smith, Marshall et al. (2023), Proc. Royal Society B — the recent correction: its grasping arms were too fragile to crack a shell, built for soft prey and speed, not crushing trilobites
Smith & Caron (2015), Nature — Hallucigenia's head, fully resolved after decades reconstructed the wrong way up
Briggs & Fortey (2005), Paleobiology — the rebuttal to Gould's "Wonderful Life": most "weird wonders" are extinct stem-group members of phyla still alive today, not separate vanished phyla
Briggs (2015), Current Biology — "they do not represent extinct higher taxa, but are early offshoots of the lineages leading to modern groups"
Zhang & Shu (2021), PalZ — "most fossils can be comfortably placed into a stem or crown group of a living phylum"
